findings.title: Failed work items are marked completed and committed
findings.body: In OrderedQueueWorker.run, complete_offset is called in a finally block, so it runs even when result_processor raises. The exception is logged and swallowed, and the commit thread then treats the offset as successfully processed and commits it. A transient processing failure therefore loses the message instead of retrying it; the new error-handling test also expects the offset not to be committed after a processing failure.

findings.title: Submit exceptions are converted into successful offsets
findings.body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches every exception from decoding, grouping, or enqueueing, then calls add_offset and complete_offset for the message. That marks the message as processed even though no work item was queued, so the offset is committed and the message is dropped. Failures should propagate or be routed to a DLQ rather than being completed.

findings.title: OffsetTracker can commit past a gap after the first commit
findings.body: get_committable_offsets starts at max(last_committed + 1, min_offset). After marking offset 100 committed, all_offsets is pruned and if the remaining set is {102, 103}, start becomes 102, so the method returns 103 and commits offset 104 even though offset 101 was never added or processed. This contradicts the class's stated guarantee and the new gap test; once the first commit occurs, a missing prior offset is no longer treated as blocking.

findings.title: Uses Python 3.13-only queue shutdown APIs
findings.body: Queue.shutdown() and queue.ShutDown were added in Python 3.13. On the older Python versions supported by this repository, q.shutdown raises AttributeError (caught and logged), leaving workers blocked in Queue.get() and making the join timeouts ineffective. Additionally, when a worker catches a processing exception, evaluating the except queue.ShutDown clause raises AttributeError and kills the worker thread.

findings.title: Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure
findings.body: Each queue is created with queue.Queue() without a maxsize, and submit always enqueues immediately. If one group or worker is slow, the consumer continues pulling Kafka messages into memory without limit. The documented 'natural backpressure when queues fill up' never happens, and a slow group can cause unbounded memory growth or an OOM.

findings.title: Shutdown does not drain queued work
findings.body: shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True before calling queue.shutdown(immediate=False). Because the worker checks that flag at the top of its loop, it exits after at most the current item and leaves any remaining queued items unprocessed, even though immediate=False is intended to allow draining. This makes the advertised graceful shutdown incomplete and leaves pending offsets uncommitted.
